doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Women in jazz and the business
title: Clora Bryant and undocumented women in jazz
summary: At a tribute event she saw video of Clora Bryant and wept that such a player is absent from jazz history.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: thing to honor women — Nancy Wilson, Clora Bryant, Jane Jarvis, Diva, and we were sponsored by a Vodka company called Gray Goose Vodka. So we did this charity event for “Dress for Success” and Clora Bryant came, she’s a trumpet player from Los Angeles. Do you know her well?
No I don’t know her well but I know the name.

Well I only knew that she can’t play anymore and I just knew her as that women that used to play trumpet. And she’s an amazing personality. And she sent us some video of her. And I started crying when I saw her videotape. She was so, so great, like on the par easily with Dizzy Gillespie and like Louis Armstrong kind of combination. Sang her brains out, danced. And I really started to cry. I was like why isn’t this woman just in the history book next to all these other guys? Because here she is, like probably one of the first Afro-American women ever on television. She was on a lot of the big T.V. talk shows playing the trumpet, she was dancing. And I saw it and I said it’s so weird that me, like crawling towards 40 and studying jazz my whole life hardly know any of the women. I mean I had no clue she played this good. Or to be so stupid that I didn’t know women in that day could play like that. I mean that’s a stupid thing to say but it’s so undocumented that it’s really hard to find information.
Yeah. You have to assume that nothing was happening because there’s nothing there to tell you about it.

Right. And then you see these little things like that kind of, and you feel bad that — I don’t know if it would have changed anything about the way I grew up, you know in studying jazz, except maybe it would have been great to see somebody, an instrumentalist, somebody besides a singer being considered a woman in jazz. It might have encouraged a lot more women to go into it or something. I don’t know.
